newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Croats force resettling Moslems to flee. [CORRECTED 20:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croats force resettling Moslems to flee. [CORRECTED 20:50 GMT]

text.p: Hundreds of Moslems who returned to their pre-war homes over the last three weeks in a Croat-controlled area of Bosnia have been forced to flee again by drunken Croat mobs, officials said on Sunday.
The refugees had been filtering back to the town of Jajce and surrounding villages, about 100 km (60 miles) northwest of Sarajevo, a spokesman for the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia (SFOR) said.

A crowd of local Croats, realising how many Moslems had returned to the area, blocked a road all day on Friday to prevent more from coming back, United Nations International Police Task Force (IPTF) spokesman Alex Ivanko said.
Local police failed to disband the crowd after it turned violent, Ivanko said, and the situation continued through Saturday into the night as Croats intimidated Moslem returnees.
Moslems and Bosnian Croats allied with each other in 1994 under a U.S. brokered deal and are now joined in a Moslem-Croat Federation which makes up half of post-war Bosnia.
However the federation is still peppered with areas populated mainly by either Bosnian Croats or Moslems.

"Groups of Croats hung around the area in the night drinking heavily and waiting for the (Moslems) to return. One empty house was seen burning in the area and an IPTF vehicle was stoned early this morning by Croats who were heavily intoxicated," Ivanko told Reuters.
He said 372 Moslems decided not to stay and moved to a police station in a nearby Moslem-controlled area.
"It is not good news of course. Jajce was one of the few areas where there was quite a substantial number of (Moslem) families who had returned to their homes over the past three weeks," Ivanko said.
"Now a very big portion of those families doesn't feel secure there. The police are not able to provide security."

Under the Dayton peace agreement which ended the Bosnian war in November 1995, all refugees in the former Yugoslavia have the right to return to their pre-war homes. However progress has been slow throughout the region.

An SFOR source (corrects from "The SFOR spokesman") said Bosnian Croats have been prevented from returning to the town of Bugojno, in a Moslem area, and were angered by the return to their area by Moslems.

On Friday in the Sarajevo suburb of Vogosca, a Serb group of refugees who had come to negotiate their possible return to the area were stoned by an angry group of Moslem women who fled the enclave of Srebrenica in 1995.
Thousands of Moslem men disappeared in Srebrenica and are believed to have been massacred by Serb soldiers who captured the town.
